title: Medium exam 6
about: Ten single-choice questions that combine two facts or ask you to trace two or three steps: escapes, `xargs`, anchored patterns, mount points, signals, `case` and checking arguments.

questions.title: Escapes in echo
questions.text: In bash, what do `echo 'a\tb'` and `echo -e 'a\tb'` print?

options.t: Both print `a`, a tab and `b`, because `\t` is always a tab.
options.why: Without `-e`, `echo` prints the backslash and the `t` as they are.

options.t: Both print `a\tb`, because single quotes block every escape.
options.why: The quotes are not what matters: `-e` makes `echo` interpret `\t`.

options.t: The first prints `a\tb`; the second prints `a`, a tab and `b`.
options.why: `-e` turns on the interpretation of backslash escapes such as `\t` and `\n`.

options.t: The first prints `a`, a tab and `b`; the second prints `a\tb`.
options.why: It is the other way round.

questions.title: Arguments that are not stdin
questions.text: You want to delete every file whose name ends in `~` under the current directory. Which command does it by sending the list of names that `find` prints to `rm`?

options.why: `rm` takes the names as arguments and does not read stdin: it complains "missing operand".
It writes the list into a file called `rm`; nothing is removed.
`xargs` reads the names from stdin and runs `rm` with them as arguments.
The pipe goes in the wrong direction: `rm` would have to produce the names.

questions.title: Patterns on a word list
questions.text: `w` holds the words `cart`, `cat`, `coat`, `cot` and `ct`, one per line. Which command prints exactly `cat` and `cot`?

options.why: `.*` is any number of characters, so it matches all five words.
`o*` repeats only the `o`: it matches `cot` and `ct`.
Exactly one character of any kind between `c` and `t`, in a line that starts and ends there.
In a basic regular expression `?` is an ordinary character, so nothing matches.

questions.title: Writing under a mount point
questions.text: `/data` holds the file `old.log`. You mount a disk that contains `new1` and `new2` on `/data`, then run `echo x > /data/new3`, and finally `umount /data`. What does `ls /data` show?

options.why: While the disk is mounted, `old.log` is hidden; and after `umount` the disk's files are gone from the tree.
Those files belong to the disk, which is no longer mounted.
Once unmounted, the original content reappears; `new3` was written on the disk, not in the directory underneath.
`umount` removes nothing; it only shows again what was under the mount point.

questions.title: Editing the command line
questions.text: Which statement about editing and history in bash is FALSE?

options.t: `Tab` completes the name of a command or file.
options.why: True.

options.t: `Ctrl+A` moves the cursor to the start of the line and `Ctrl+E` to the end.
options.why: True.

options.t: The up arrow retrieves the previous command from the history.
options.why: True.

options.t: `Ctrl+R` and a few characters finds the oldest command that contains them.
options.why: False: it finds the most recent one, and pressing `Ctrl+R` again moves to the next most recent.

questions.title: What the kernel does
questions.text: Which statement about what happens after the boot loader hands over the control is FALSE?

options.t: The kernel initialises memory management and the interrupt vector of the CPU.
options.why: True: these are early tasks of the kernel.

options.t: The initrd is a temporary RAM disk with the drivers and tools needed to find the real root filesystem.
options.why: True: it is used until the root filesystem can be mounted.

options.t: The kernel finally looks for the initial process and starts it with PID 1.
options.why: True: it is the process that brings up the services.

options.t: The idle process, with PID 0, is the one that starts the services.
options.why: False: PID 0 is the idle process of the kernel; the services are started by PID 1.

questions.title: Checking the arguments
questions.text:
`need3.sh` contains:
```
if [ $# -ne 3 ]; then echo "usage: $0 src dst mode" >&2; exit 1; fi
echo ok
```
You run `bash need3.sh onlyone 2> err.txt; echo "status=$?"; wc -l < err.txt`. What is printed on the screen?

options.t: `usage: need3.sh src dst mode`, then `status=1` and `0`
options.why: The usage message was written to stderr, so it went into `err.txt` and not to the screen.
One argument is not three: the test fails and the script ends before `echo ok`.
The message went to `err.txt` (one line), and the script ended with status 1.
`exit 1` sets the status of the script to 1.

questions.title: Seeing the bytes
questions.text: Which command prints the content of the file `data` as hexadecimal values, one per byte?

options.why: `-c` shows the bytes as characters, with escapes such as `\n`.
`-t x1` selects hexadecimal with one byte per value.
It lists the bytes that differ between two files; it does not dump one.
It compares two text files line by line.

questions.title: A case with patterns

options.why: `b|c` means exactly `b` or exactly `c`; `bc` is neither, so it falls to `*`.
`c` is one of the alternatives of `b|c`.
`abc` matches `a*`, `c` matches `b|c`, and `bc` only matches `*`.
`abc` starts with `a`, so the first pattern matches.

questions.title: A process that ignores TERM
questions.text: A script has been written to ignore SIGTERM and keep running. You run `kill 4321` on it, wait a second, and then run `kill -9 4321`. What happens?

options.t: The first `kill` ends it, and the second reports that the process does not exist.
options.why: SIGTERM can be caught or ignored, and here it is ignored.

options.t: Both signals are ignored, because a process can ignore any signal.
options.why: SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored.

options.t: It is still running after the first `kill`, and the second one ends it.
options.why: `kill` sends SIGTERM (15) by default; `-9` sends SIGKILL, which the process cannot refuse.

options.t: The first `kill` stops it temporarily, and the second one makes it continue.
options.why: Neither signal suspends it; the first has no visible effect.
